topic-1-1-1.foundation: From the axioms \(P\), “\(P\) implies \(Q\),” and “\(Q\) implies \(R\),” with modus ponens as the only rule of inference, write a proof of \(R\). Give the justification of each line.
topic-1-1-1.application: Prove that the sum of an even integer and an odd integer is odd, giving the justification for each step.
topic-1-1-1.challenge: A checker accepts every line of a proof. Show by an example that the conclusion can still be false, and say exactly what the accepted proof establishes.

topic-1-1-2.foundation: A system has the axioms \(P\) and “\(P\) implies not \(P\),” and the rule modus ponens. Is it consistent?
topic-1-1-2.application: Suppose a system also has the rule “from \(A\) and not \(A\), infer any statement \(B\).” Show that if the system is inconsistent, it proves every statement.
topic-1-1-2.challenge: Hilbert hoped to prove that systems are consistent. Show that a consistency proof carried out inside the same system \(S\) could not settle the doubt, by showing that an inconsistent \(S\) of the kind in the previous problem proves the statement “\(S\) is consistent.”

topic-1-1-3.foundation: Strings over the alphabet \(\{a,b\}\) are listed by length, starting with the empty string, and alphabetically within each length. Write the first seven strings, and give the position of \(ab\).
topic-1-1-3.application: A proof search lists candidate strings over a two-symbol alphabet in this order and checks each one. If the shortest proof of a statement has length \(5\), at most how many candidates are checked before a proof is found? Why can such a bound not be computed in advance for an arbitrary statement?
topic-1-1-3.challenge: Suppose a theory is consistent, its axioms can be listed by an algorithm, and it is complete: for every sentence \(P\), it proves \(P\) or it proves not \(P\). Show that searching for a proof of \(P\) and a proof of not \(P\) in alternation is a decision procedure for provability.

topic-1-2-1.foundation: Run Euclid’s algorithm on \((91,35)\), writing each division and each pair.
topic-1-2-1.application: Run Euclid’s algorithm on \((21,13)\). How many divisions does it take, and why does this pair make the second entry decrease slowly?
topic-1-2-1.challenge: Give a procedure on pairs of positive integers that keeps the greatest common divisor unchanged at every step but never stops, and another that always stops but can return a wrong answer. What does this show about the two arguments for Euclid’s algorithm?

topic-1-2-2.foundation: Euclid’s algorithm divides by repeated subtraction. It is paused in the middle of dividing \(48\) by \(18\), after one subtraction has given \(30\). What must the configuration record so that the computation can resume?
topic-1-2-2.application: Write the run of Euclid’s algorithm from \((30,18)\) as a sequence of configurations. Find two other pairs whose runs reach \((18,12)\) after one step.
topic-1-2-2.challenge: Describe all pairs from which Euclid’s algorithm reaches \((18,12)\) in one step. What does the answer imply about running the algorithm backward?

topic-1-2-3.foundation: A machine has a running state \(q\) and a halting state \(h\). In \(q\), reading \(1\), it writes \(1\), moves right, and stays in \(q\); reading a blank, it halts. Started on the leftmost \(1\) of a tape holding \(111\), list its configurations until it halts.
topic-1-2-3.application: Change the machine so that, reading a blank in state \(q\), it writes \(1\) and halts. What does the new machine compute on a block of \(n\) ones, and how many steps does it take?
topic-1-2-3.challenge: Design a machine that, started on the leftmost symbol of a block of ones, halts in a state marked “even” if the block has an even number of ones and “odd” otherwise. Give its rule table and trace it on \(111\).

topic-1-3-1.foundation: A programming language \(L\) can simulate every Turing machine, and a Turing machine can simulate every program of \(L\). Which functions does \(L\) compute? Is this conclusion a theorem or an instance of the Church–Turing thesis?
topic-1-3-1.application: Classify each statement as a theorem or as the Church–Turing thesis: (a) lambda calculus and Turing machines compute the same functions; (b) every function computable by an effective mechanical method is Turing-computable; (c) every recursive function is Turing-computable.
topic-1-3-1.challenge: Show that some functions from nonnegative integers to \(\{0,1\}\) are computed by no Turing machine. Turing machines can be listed as \(M_0,M_1,M_2,\dots\), since each has a finite description.

topic-1-3-2.foundation: Decide, by inspecting each program, whether it halts on the input \(x=5\): (a) while \(x\gt 0\), set \(x:=x-1\); (b) while \(x\neq0\), set \(x:=x-2\); (c) repeat forever: do nothing.
topic-1-3-2.application: A proposed halting test runs a program for a million steps. It answers “halts” if the program stops and “never halts” otherwise. Give a program on which this test is wrong. Would replacing a million by a larger fixed number repair it?
topic-1-3-2.challenge: Show that no algorithm decides, for every program \(P\), whether \(P\) halts when given the input \(0\). Use the undecidability of the halting problem: from a pair \((P,x)\), construct a program that ignores its own input.

topic-1-3-3.foundation: A theory has the single axiom \(P\) and the rule modus ponens, and its sentences are built from \(P\) and \(Q\). Is \(Q\) provable? Is not \(Q\) provable? Is the theory complete?
topic-1-3-3.application: A sentence \(G\) is neither provable nor refutable in a consistent theory \(T\). Show that both \(T\) with \(G\) added as an axiom and \(T\) with not \(G\) added are consistent. You may use the fact that if \(T\) with an added axiom \(A\) proves a contradiction, then \(T\) proves not \(A\).
topic-1-3-3.challenge: Suppose an algorithm extends a consistent, effectively axiomatized theory of arithmetic step by step, each time adding a sentence that the current theory leaves undecided. Show that the combined theory, with all the added axioms together, is still incomplete if it is consistent.

topic-1-4-1.foundation: A rule on the configurations \(A,B,C,D\) sends \(A\to B\), \(B\to C\), \(C\to D\), and \(D\to B\). Is it deterministic? Which configurations have more than one predecessor, and which have none?
topic-1-4-1.application: Run the same rule for six steps from each of \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), and \(D\). Which starting configurations end at the same configuration after six steps?
topic-1-4-1.challenge: Prove that a deterministic, one-to-one rule on finitely many configurations is onto, and that every run of such a rule eventually returns to its starting configuration.

topic-1-4-2.foundation: Which of these operations on two bits lose information: \((x,y)\mapsto x\land y\); \((x,y)\mapsto(x,x\oplus y)\); \((x,y)\mapsto(y,x)\); \((x,y)\mapsto x\oplus y\)?
topic-1-4-2.application: Keep both inputs and store the AND in an extra bit \(t\) that starts at \(0\): \((x,y,t)\mapsto(x,y,t\oplus(x\land y))\). List the outputs for the four inputs with \(t=0\), and show that the map can be undone.
topic-1-4-2.challenge: A computation maps \(n\)-bit inputs to a single output bit. Show that at least \(2^{n-1}\) inputs share an output. If the computation keeps some bits besides its output, how many must it keep, at least, to become one-to-one, and how many always suffice?

topic-2-1-1.foundation: Write \(13\) in binary with four bits, and decode \(1011\) as an unsigned binary integer.
topic-2-1-1.application: An integer \(N\) is written in binary and, alternatively, in unary, as \(N\) marks. For \(N=1000\), compare the two input lengths. How does a procedure that takes \(N\) steps compare with each length?
topic-2-1-1.challenge: Show that any encoding of the integers \(0,1,\dots,M-1\) by bit strings of one fixed length \(n\) needs \(n\geq\log_2M\).

topic-2-1-2.foundation: Write the truth table of the majority function on three bits, which outputs \(1\) when at least two of its inputs are \(1\).
topic-2-1-2.application: How many Boolean functions of two bits are there? List those that output \(1\) on exactly one input.
topic-2-1-2.challenge: Show that there are \(2^{2^n}\) Boolean functions of \(n\) bits. For \(n=10\), show that fewer than one function in a thousand can be described by a string of fewer than \(1014\) bits.

topic-2-1-3.foundation: Evaluate \((1+x)(1+y)\) modulo two for all four inputs. Which function is it?
topic-2-1-3.application: Build the polynomial of XOR from its truth table using detectors, and simplify it.
topic-2-1-3.challenge: Show that the polynomial of the three-bit majority function is \(xy+yz+xz\) modulo two.

topic-2-2-1.foundation: Evaluate the circuit for \(x+y+xy\), built from one AND gate and two XOR gates, on the input \(10\), giving the bit on every wire.
topic-2-2-1.application: Build a circuit for majority, \(xy+yz+xz\), from AND and XOR gates. How many gates does it use?
topic-2-2-1.challenge: The parity function \(x_1+x_2+\dots+x_n\pmod2\) equals \(1\) on half of its inputs. How many detectors does the truth-table construction add, and how many XOR gates does the simplified polynomial need?

topic-2-2-2.foundation: Compute \(\operatorname{NAND}(a,b)\) for all four inputs. Use the table to check that \(\operatorname{NAND}\bigl(\operatorname{NAND}(a,b),\operatorname{NAND}(a,b)\bigr)=a\land b\).
topic-2-2-2.application: Build OR from NAND gates, and verify the construction on all four inputs.
topic-2-2-2.challenge: Show that circuits of AND and XOR gates, with no constant inputs, cannot compute NOT, but that adding the constant \(1\) makes the set universal.

topic-2-2-3.foundation: For OR on two bits, list the inputs that share each output. Can the inputs be recovered from the output?
topic-2-2-3.application: A circuit computes \((x,y)\mapsto(x\land y,\;x\lor y)\). Is this map one-to-one? Which inputs collide?
topic-2-2-3.challenge: The map \((x,y)\mapsto(x,\,x\oplus y)\) is computed by copying \(x\) and feeding \(x\) and \(y\) into an XOR gate, which on its own loses information. Show that the map is one-to-one, and explain where the information discarded by the XOR gate survives.

topic-2-3-1.foundation: Compute \(k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2\) at \(T=300\) K, with \(k_{\mathrm B}=1.38\times10^{-23}\) J/K.
topic-2-3-1.application: A processor erases \(10^{18}\) bits per second at \(300\) K. What minimum power does Landauer’s principle require? Compare it with a processor that uses \(50\) W.
topic-2-3-1.challenge: Erasing a bit that is \(0\) with probability \(p\) and \(1\) with probability \(1-p\) has the minimum cost \(H\,k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2\), where \(H=-p\log_2p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)\). Compute \(H\) for \(p=0.9\), and compare the cost with that of an unbiased bit and a known bit.

topic-2-3-2.foundation: Which of these are logically reversible: NOT; AND; \((x,y)\mapsto(x,x\oplus y)\); a reset to \(0\)?
topic-2-3-2.application: A device implements NOT but dissipates \(10^{-18}\) J per operation, while the Landauer bound at \(300\) K is about \(2.9\times10^{-21}\) J. Does the dissipation contradict the reversibility of NOT? Does Landauer’s principle require any dissipation for NOT?
topic-2-3-2.challenge: Show that a reversible map on \(n\)-bit strings is a permutation of the \(2^n\) strings. For \(n=2\), count the reversible maps and compare with the number of all maps from two bits to two bits.

topic-2-3-3.foundation: Write the outputs of \(U_f:(x,y,t)\mapsto(x,y,t\oplus(x\lor y))\) for the four inputs with \(t=0\).
topic-2-3-3.application: For OR, apply \(U_f\) to \((1,0,1)\), then apply it again. A programmer expected the target to contain \(f(1,0)=1\) after the first call. What assumption did they overlook?
topic-2-3-3.challenge: For a function \(f\) from \(n\)-bit strings to \(m\)-bit strings, define \(U_f(x,t)=(x,t\oplus f(x))\), where \(t\) has \(m\) bits and \(\oplus\) acts bit by bit. Prove that \(U_f\) is its own inverse for every \(f\).

topic-2-4-1.foundation: Apply CNOT with the second bit as control and the first as target to \(00\), \(01\), \(10\), and \(11\).
topic-2-4-1.application: Apply three CNOT gates in turn to \((a,b)\): control the first bit and target the second, then control the second and target the first, then control the first and target the second. Show that the result is \((b,a)\).
topic-2-4-1.challenge: A controlled operation keeps a control bit \(c\) and applies a map \(g_c\) to the target. Prove that it is reversible when \(g_0\) and \(g_1\) are both reversible, and give its inverse. Show by an example that it is not reversible if \(g_1\) is a reset.

topic-2-4-2.foundation: Apply the Toffoli gate to all eight inputs \((a,b,c)\). Which inputs change?
topic-2-4-2.application: Using Toffoli gates and extra bits set to fixed values, compute \(a\land b\), \(\neg a\), and \(a\oplus b\). Specify the inputs of each gate.
topic-2-4-2.challenge: Prove that every output bit of a circuit of CNOT and NOT gates is a sum modulo two of input bits, possibly plus \(1\). Conclude that such circuits cannot compute \(a\land b\).

topic-2-4-3.foundation: In the three-bit AND computation with workspace \(w\) and output \(t\), list the five bits \((x,y,z,w,t)\) after each of the three Toffoli gates for the input \((1,1,0)\).
topic-2-4-3.application: Compute the AND of four bits \(x,y,z,u\) with Toffoli gates, two workspace bits that start at \(0\), and one output bit, and return the workspace to \(0\). List the gates in order.
topic-2-4-3.challenge: A reversible computation \(A\) maps \((x,0,0)\) to \((x,f(x),g(x))\). Show that applying \(A\), then copying the answer register into a fresh register with CNOT gates, then applying \(A^{-1}\), produces \((x,0,0;f(x))\) for every input \(x\).

topic-3-1-1.foundation: A two-bit register has configurations \(00,01,10,11\). Write the weights of its state when (a) the register is known to hold \(10\); (b) the first bit is known to be \(1\) and the second could be either; (c) both bits were set by independent fair coins.
topic-3-1-1.application: Someone describes a bit by the weights \(v_0=v_1=1\). Can these weights be probabilities? What do they say about the bit, and what do they leave unsaid? Give two different probability states that are consistent with them.
topic-3-1-1.challenge: A register has \(k\) bits. A possibility state gives each configuration weight \(0\) or \(1\), with at least one weight \(1\). How many possibility states are there? How many probability states are there? Which probability states are consistent with the possibility state in which every configuration is possible?

topic-3-1-2.foundation: A rule on the configurations \(0,1,2\) sends \(0\to1\), \(1\to2\), and \(2\to0\). Draw its state diagram and write the run from \(0\) for four steps.
topic-3-1-2.application: For the same rule, draw the time-expanded diagram for the times \(t=0,1,2\). How many arrows does it contain, and which path is the run from \(2\)?
topic-3-1-2.challenge: A rule on \(m\) configurations has \(a\) arrows in its state diagram. How many arrows does its time-expanded diagram have for the times \(0,1,\dots,t\)? Show that the runs of \(t\) steps are exactly the paths from time \(0\) to time \(t\), and explain why the time-expanded diagram never contains a cycle, even when the state diagram does.

topic-3-1-3.foundation: On two bits, the rule SWAP exchanges the bits: \(01\to10\) and \(10\to01\), while \(00\) and \(11\) stay as they are. Write the two-step run from \(01\). Is SWAP deterministic? Is it reversible?
topic-3-1-3.application: On the configurations \(0,1,2,3\), the rule INC adds \(1\) modulo \(4\), and the rule HALVE replaces \(n\) by \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), the integer part of \(n/2\). Draw both state diagrams, write the two-step runs from \(3\), and decide which rule is reversible.
topic-3-1-3.challenge: Prove that a deterministic rule on finitely many configurations is reversible exactly when every configuration has at least one incoming arrow. Then show that the statement fails for the rule \(n\mapsto\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) on all nonnegative integers.

topic-3-1-4.foundation: A rule on \(\{0,1\}\) allows \(0\to1\), \(1\to0\), and \(1\to1\), and forbids \(0\to0\). List the possible two-step runs from \(0\), and the configurations reachable at time \(2\).
topic-3-1-4.application: For the same rule, list the possible three-step runs from \(0\). Which configurations are reachable at time \(3\), and by how many paths?
topic-3-1-4.challenge: On the configurations \(0,1,\dots,k\), a rule allows \(i\to i\) and \(i\to i+1\) for \(i\lt k\), and only \(k\to k\) at \(k\). Show that \(k\) is reachable from \(0\) at time \(t\) exactly when \(t\geq k\), and that the number of paths from \(0\) to \(k\) at time \(t\) is \(\binom tk\).

topic-3-1-5.foundation: A step keeps the bit with probability \(2/3\) and flips it with probability \(1/3\). Starting from \(0\), compute \(P(c_2=0)\) by listing the paths that end at \(0\).
topic-3-1-5.application: For the same rule, compute \(P(c_3=0)\) from \(0\). Check your answer against the formula \(P(c_t=0)=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\left(\tfrac13\right)^t\).
topic-3-1-5.challenge: Prove the formula \(P(c_t=0)=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\left(\tfrac13\right)^t\) for the rule above, and describe what happens to the run’s memory of its starting configuration as \(t\) grows.

topic-3-2-1.foundation: Under the rule that keeps the bit with probability \(2/3\) and flips it with probability \(1/3\), what is the weight of the path \(0\to0\to1\to1\)?
topic-3-2-1.application: A nondeterministic rule on \(\{0,1\}\) allows \(0\to0\), \(0\to1\), and \(1\to1\), and forbids \(1\to0\). Using the product rule with weights \(1\) and \(0\), decide which of the eight three-step paths from \(0\) are possible.
topic-3-2-1.challenge: The product rule for probabilities assumes the Markov property. Find a two-step random process on \(\{0,1\}\) in which the probability of the path \(0\to1\to0\), given the start \(0\), differs from \(P(c_1=1\mid c_0=0)\,P(c_2=0\mid c_1=1)\).

topic-3-2-2.foundation: Under KEEP-OR-FLIP, how many possible paths lead from \(0\) to \(1\) in three steps, and what does the count tell us?
topic-3-2-2.application: A rule has \(P(0\mid0)=2/3\), \(P(1\mid0)=1/3\), \(P(0\mid1)=1/4\), and \(P(1\mid1)=3/4\). Use the sum rule to compute the four two-step weights \(w(i\Rightarrow k)\), and check that the weights from each start add to \(1\).
topic-3-2-2.challenge: Prove that, for any probabilistic rule, the two-step weights \(w(i\Rightarrow k)\) given by the sum and product rules add to \(1\) over \(k\). What does this show about composing two probabilistic steps?

topic-3-2-3.foundation: Apply one step of COIN, and separately one step of NOT, to the state with weights \(0.9\) on \(0\) and \(0.1\) on \(1\).
topic-3-2-3.application: For the rule with \(P(0\mid0)=2/3\), \(P(1\mid0)=1/3\), \(P(0\mid1)=1/4\), and \(P(1\mid1)=3/4\), find the distribution that one step leaves unchanged.
topic-3-2-3.challenge: Prove that a probabilistic rule on finitely many configurations can be undone by another probabilistic rule only if it is deterministic and reversible.

topic-3-3-1.foundation: A path has arrow weights \(-1/2\), \(1/3\), and \(-3/4\). What is its weight?
topic-3-3-1.application: A starting configuration has weight \(-2\). A path from it has arrow weights \(1/2\) and \(-1/3\). What contribution reaches the endpoint?
topic-3-3-1.challenge: If the sign of one nonzero arrow weight on a path is reversed, how does the path weight change? What if two arrow occurrences change sign?

topic-3-3-2.foundation: Three paths to the same endpoint contribute \(1/3\), \(-1/2\), and \(1/6\). What is the total? Does it imply that no path reaches the endpoint?
topic-3-3-2.application: In the two-path diagram, set \(a=b=c=1/2\). Find the total at \(k\) for \(d=1/2\), \(d=-1/4\), and \(d=-1/2\).
topic-3-3-2.challenge: Two paths to \(0\) contribute \(1/4\) each, and two paths to \(1\) contribute \(-1/4\) each. What are the final state weights? Can any contributions cancel?

topic-3-3-3.application: Draw the two-step paths from \(1\) under \(H\). Compute the contribution of each path and the final weights.
topic-3-3-3.challenge: Replace the negative arrow of \(H\) by \(+1/\sqrt2\). Starting at \(0\), find the weights after two steps. Explain why this modified step cannot be reversible.

topic-3-4-1.foundation: A symmetric step has stay-weight \(a\) and switch-weight \(b\). Write the two-step weights for returning and switching. Why can real \(a,b\) not make two steps equal NOT?
topic-3-4-1.application: For the operation \(S\) with \(S(0\to0)=S(1\to1)=(1+i)/2\) and \(S(0\to1)=S(1\to0)=(1-i)/2\), compute the two-step weights from \(1\) to \(0\) and to \(1\).
topic-3-4-1.challenge: Find every operation with \(S(0\to0)=S(1\to1)=a\) and \(S(0\to1)=S(1\to0)=b\) whose two steps give NOT. Show in particular that \(a\) and \(b\) cannot both be real.

topic-3-4-2.foundation: Two paths reach an outcome with amplitudes \(1/2\) and \(i/2\). What is its probability? Is the interference constructive, destructive, or neither?
topic-3-4-2.application: Two paths contribute \(0.6\) and \(-0.2\) to an outcome. Compare the probability obtained by adding first with the result of squaring first.
topic-3-4-2.challenge: Start with amplitudes \((1/\sqrt2,e^{i\phi}/\sqrt2)\) and apply \(H\). The probability of \(0\) is \((1+\cos\phi)/2\). Which values of \(\phi\) give the same probabilities, and what extra operation could distinguish them?

topic-3-4-3.foundation: In the record experiment, find the probability of each of the four final configurations, and the probability that the record shows \(1\).
topic-3-4-3.application: Check the final state \(\tfrac12(\ket{00}+\ket{10}+\ket{01}-\ket{11})\) by applying \(H\) to the qubit in \(\ket{00}\) and in \(\ket{11}\) separately.
topic-3-4-3.challenge: Replace the CNOT by an operation that records the path only partly: it leaves \(\ket{00}\) unchanged and sends \(\ket{10}\) to \(\ket1(\cos\alpha\ket0+\sin\alpha\ket1)\). Show that the qubit then gives \(1\) at the end with probability \((1-\cos\alpha)/2\), and interpret the cases \(\alpha=0\) and \(\alpha=\pi/2\).

topic-4-1-1.foundation: Write \(\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\ket0+i\sqrt{\tfrac23}\ket1\) as a column vector, and check that its coordinates satisfy the condition for a state vector.
topic-4-1-1.application: With the two-qubit configurations ordered \(00,01,10,11\), write \((\ket{00}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\) as a column vector, and give the probability of each configuration.
topic-4-1-1.challenge: Find numbers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(\ket0=a\,\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}+b\,\tfrac{\ket0-\ket1}{\sqrt2}\). Relative to which basis is \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\) a superposition, and relative to which is it not?

topic-4-1-2.foundation: An operation has weights \(w(0\to0)=0\), \(w(0\to1)=i\), \(w(1\to0)=-i\), and \(w(1\to1)=0\). Write its matrix, and apply it to \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\).
topic-4-1-2.application: Compute the matrices \(XZ\) and \(ZX\), and apply each to \(\ket0\). Does the order of the operations matter?
topic-4-1-2.challenge: A proposed rule sends \(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\) to \(\alpha\ket0+2\beta\ket1\), rescaled so that the squared magnitudes add to \(1\). Show that the rule is not linear by comparing its action on \(\ket0\), \(\ket1\), and \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\).

topic-4-1-3.foundation: Compute \(\braket\phi\psi\) for \(\ket\phi=(\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\) and \(\ket\psi=(\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). Are the two states orthogonal?
topic-4-1-3.application: Find the adjoints of \(\operatorname{diag}(1,i)\) and of \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Which of the two matrices is unitary?
topic-4-1-3.challenge: Using \(\braket\phi{A\psi}=\braket{A^\dagger\phi}\psi\), prove that \((AB)^\dagger=B^\dagger A^\dagger\). Conclude that the product of two unitaries is unitary.

topic-4-2-1.foundation: Normalize \(\ket0+2i\ket1\), and give the probabilities of a computational-basis measurement.
topic-4-2-1.application: Write the state \((i\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\) in the form \(\cos\tfrac\theta2\ket0+e^{i\phi}\sin\tfrac\theta2\ket1\), after removing a global phase.
topic-4-2-1.challenge: Show that \(\ket\psi\) and \(e^{i\gamma}\ket\psi\) give the same probabilities for every sequence of operations followed by a computational-basis measurement. Then show that \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\) and \((\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\) do not differ by a global phase.

topic-4-2-2.foundation: Measure \((\ket0+2i\ket1)/\sqrt5\) in the computational basis. Give the probability of each outcome and the state after it.
topic-4-2-2.application: A qubit in \((\sqrt3/2)\ket0+(1/2)\ket1\) is measured twice in a row. Find the probabilities of the four sequences of outcomes \(00\), \(01\), \(10\), and \(11\).
topic-4-2-2.challenge: Start from \(\ket0\). Apply \(H\), measure, apply \(H\), and measure again. Find the probabilities of the four pairs of outcomes, and compare with applying \(H\) twice and measuring once.

topic-4-2-3.foundation: A preparation gives outcome \(1\) with probability \(0.3\). In \(100\) independent runs, what is the expected number of \(1\)s, and its standard deviation \(\sqrt{Np(1-p)}\)?
topic-4-2-3.application: For \(p=1/2\), how many independent runs are needed for the standard deviation of the observed fraction, \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/N}\), to be at most \(0.01\)?
topic-4-2-3.challenge: Someone measures a single qubit, prepared in \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\), a hundred times in a row, obtains \(0\) every time, and concludes that the state was \(\ket0\). What do the data actually show? Design an experiment that distinguishes \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\) from \(\ket0\).

topic-4-3-1.challenge: Let \(\ket{\pm i}=(\ket0\pm i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). Show that these two vectors form an orthonormal basis, and write \(\ket+\) in it.

topic-4-3-2.foundation: Measure \((\sqrt3/2)\ket0+(1/2)\ket1\) in the \(\pm\) basis. Give the probability of each outcome.
topic-4-3-2.application: Let \(\ket{\pm i}=(\ket0\pm i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). Which operations, applied before a computational-basis measurement, measure a qubit in the basis \(\{\ket{+i},\ket{-i}\}\)? Check your answer on \(\ket{+i}\).
topic-4-3-2.challenge: Let \(U\) be the unitary with columns \(\ket{u_j}\). Show that applying \(U^\dagger\) and then measuring in the computational basis gives outcome \(j\) with probability \(|\braket{u_j}\psi|^2\).

topic-4-3-3.foundation: Check that \(H\) preserves the overlap of \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\).
topic-4-3-3.application: The matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is not unitary. Find two states whose overlap it changes.
topic-4-3-3.challenge: Prove that a matrix that preserves the norm of every vector preserves every inner product. Expand \(\|\phi+\psi\|^2\) and \(\|\phi+i\psi\|^2\).

topic-4-4-1.foundation: Show that \(\ket{+i}=(\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\) and \(\ket{-i}=(\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\) are eigenvectors of \(Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}\), and find their eigenvalues.
topic-4-4-1.application: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(H\).
topic-4-4-1.challenge: Prove that every eigenvalue of a unitary has magnitude \(1\), and that eigenvectors of a unitary with different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

topic-4-4-2.application: The observable \(Z\) reports \(+1\) for \(\ket0\) and \(-1\) for \(\ket1\). Find its average value, \(\sum_ja_jp_j\), on \((\sqrt3/2)\ket0+(1/2)\ket1\) and on \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\).
topic-4-4-2.challenge: An observable on three basis states has value \(0\) on \(\ket0,\ket1\) and value \(1\) on \(\ket2\). For \(\ket\psi=(\ket0+\ket1+\ket2)/\sqrt3\), find the probabilities and the state after obtaining \(0\). Why would measuring the full basis and merely hiding the distinction between \(0\) and \(1\) be a different operation?

topic-4-4-3.foundation: Which of these pairs can be distinguished perfectly by one measurement: \(\{\ket0,\ket1\}\); \(\{\ket+,\ket-\}\); \(\{\ket0,\ket+\}\); \(\{\ket+,\ket{+i}\}\), where \(\ket{+i}=(\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\)?
topic-4-4-3.application: A qubit is \(\ket0\) or \(\ket+\), each with probability \(1/2\). We measure in the computational basis and guess \(\ket+\) when the outcome is \(1\) and \(\ket0\) when it is \(0\). Find the probability of guessing correctly.
topic-4-4-3.challenge: Prove that two pure states can be distinguished perfectly by a measurement exactly when they are orthogonal: give a measurement when they are, and show that none exists when they are not.

topic-5-1-1.challenge: Show that \(\braket{a\otimes b}{c\otimes d}=\braket ac\braket bd\) for vectors of two coordinates, and deduce that the tensor product of two unit vectors is a unit vector.

topic-5-1-2.foundation: Is \((\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}+\ket{11})/2\) a product state? If so, factor it.
topic-5-1-2.application: Factor \((\ket{00}-\ket{01}+\ket{10}-\ket{11})/2\), and find the probability that the second qubit gives \(0\).
topic-5-1-2.challenge: Show that a two-qubit state with amplitudes \(\alpha_{00},\alpha_{01},\alpha_{10},\alpha_{11}\) is a product state exactly when \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\).

topic-5-1-3.foundation: How many amplitudes describe a general state of \(10\) qubits? How many bits does a measurement of all \(10\) qubits return?
topic-5-1-3.application: A classical simulation stores each amplitude as two \(8\)-byte numbers. How much memory does a general \(40\)-qubit state need?
topic-5-1-3.challenge: A product state of \(n\) qubits is described by \(n\) pairs of amplitudes. Show that applying one one-qubit operation to each qubit of a product state can be simulated with work proportional to \(n\). What does this show about the size of the state space as a source of difficulty?

topic-5-2-1.foundation: Apply \(H\) to the first qubit of \(\ket{10}\), then CNOT with the first qubit as control. Which state results?
topic-5-2-1.application: Apply the same circuit to \(\ket{01}\) and to \(\ket{11}\).
topic-5-2-1.challenge: Show that the four states produced from \(\ket{00},\ket{01},\ket{10},\ket{11}\) form an orthonormal basis, and give a circuit that turns each of them back into its label.

topic-5-2-2.application: For which real numbers \(\varepsilon\) is \((\ket{00}+\varepsilon\ket{11})/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\) a product state?
topic-5-2-2.challenge: For a two-qubit state in which both outcomes of the first qubit are possible, measure the first qubit in the computational basis. Show that the state is entangled exactly when the conditional state of the second qubit depends on the outcome.

topic-5-2-3.application: For \((\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt3\), compute the joint probabilities, both marginal distributions, and \(p(\text{second}=1\mid\text{first}=0)\).
topic-5-2-3.challenge: Both qubits of \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) are measured in the basis \(\ket{u_0}=\cos\theta\ket0+\sin\theta\ket1\), \(\ket{u_1}=-\sin\theta\ket0+\cos\theta\ket1\). Show that the two results agree with certainty, for every \(\theta\).

topic-5-3-1.application: For which states \(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\) does CNOT turn \((\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1)\ket0\) into two copies, \((\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1)\otimes(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1)\)?
topic-5-3-1.challenge: A unitary \(U\) copies both basis states: \(U\ket0\ket0=\ket0\ket0\) and \(U\ket1\ket0=\ket1\ket1\). Show that, whatever \(U\) does on other inputs, it sends \(\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\ket0\) to an entangled state.

topic-5-3-2.foundation: Compute \(\braket0+\) and \(\braket{00}{++}\). Why do these values rule out a unitary that copies both \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\)?
topic-5-3-2.application: Show that a unitary can copy each of the two states \(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\) into a register prepared in \(\ket0\). Give one.
topic-5-3-2.challenge: A cloning machine may change its own state: \(U\ket\psi\ket0\ket e=\ket\psi\ket\psi\ket{e_\psi}\), where the final machine state \(\ket{e_\psi}\) may depend on \(\ket\psi\). Show that it can still clone two states only if they are orthogonal or equal up to phase.

topic-5-3-3.foundation: Alice and Bob share \(\ket{\Phi^+}\). Alice measures her qubit and does not report the result. What is the probability that Bob obtains \(0\) in a computational-basis measurement?
topic-5-3-3.application: Alice applies \(X\) to her qubit of \(\ket{\Phi^+}\), without measuring. Find the new joint state and Bob’s computational-basis probabilities.
topic-5-3-3.challenge: Alice measures her half of \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) in either the computational basis or the \(\pm\) basis, without reporting her result. Bob tests for any normalized state \(\ket v=a\ket0+b\ket1\). Show that his probability of success is \(1/2\) for either choice. Why is this stronger than checking only Bob’s computational-basis outcomes?

topic-5-4-1.foundation: In teleportation, how many qubits does each party hold at the start? Write the initial three-qubit state for \(\ket\psi=\ket1\).
topic-5-4-1.application: For \(\ket\psi=\ket1\), apply Alice’s CNOT and \(H\), and group the result by the configuration of Alice’s two qubits.
topic-5-4-1.challenge: Suppose Alice sends Bob only the bit \(m\), and Bob applies \(Z^m\). Show that for \(\ket\psi=\ket0\) his qubit is wrong with probability \(1/2\).

topic-5-4-2.foundation: Alice obtains \((m,n)=(1,0)\). Which state does Bob hold, and which correction does he apply?
topic-5-4-2.application: For \(\ket\psi=\ket+\) and Alice’s result \((1,1)\), write Bob’s state before correction, and check that the correction restores \(\ket+\).
topic-5-4-2.challenge: Bob applies his corrections in the wrong order: \(Z^m\) first, then \(X^n\). Show that he still obtains \(\ket\psi\), up to a global phase.

topic-5-4-3.foundation: Before the classical bits arrive, what is the probability that Bob obtains \(0\) when measuring his qubit, for \(\ket\psi=\ket0\)?
topic-5-4-3.application: Show that, before the bits arrive, Bob obtains \(0\) with probability \(1/2\) for every input \(\ket\psi=\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\).
topic-5-4-3.challenge: After Bob’s correction, write the three-qubit state for a particular measurement result \((m,n)\). Do Alice’s qubits retain a second copy? Explain the scope of your conclusion.

topic-6-1-1.foundation: List the four functions \(f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}\) as pairs \((f(0),f(1))\), and classify each as constant or balanced.
topic-6-1-1.application: Among the functions \(f:\{0,1\}^2\to\{0,1\}\), how many are constant, how many are balanced (output \(1\) on exactly half the inputs), and how many are neither?
topic-6-1-1.challenge: For \(f\) on \(n\)-bit inputs, promised to be constant or balanced, show that a deterministic classical algorithm can decide which with \(2^{n-1}+1\) queries, and that \(2^{n-1}\) queries do not always suffice.

topic-6-1-2.foundation: A classical algorithm queries \(f(1)\) and receives \(1\). Which of the four functions remain possible?
topic-6-1-2.application: For \(f\) on two-bit inputs, promised constant or balanced, an algorithm queries \(f(00)\) and \(f(01)\). If they differ it answers “balanced”; otherwise it makes one more query. Complete the algorithm, and give its number of queries in the worst case.
topic-6-1-2.challenge: Show that no one-query classical algorithm for \(f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}\), even one that chooses its query at random, is correct with probability greater than \(1/2\) on every function.

topic-6-1-3.foundation: Write the action of \(U_f\) on the four basis states for \(f=(1,0)\), that is, \(f(0)=1\) and \(f(1)=0\).
topic-6-1-3.application: Write the matrix of \(U_f\) for \(f=(0,1)\) in the order \(00,01,10,11\), and check that it is unitary.
topic-6-1-3.challenge: Show that the map \(\ket{x,y}\mapsto\ket{x,f(x)}\), which overwrites the target, is not unitary for any \(f\), and that \(\ket x\mapsto\ket{f(x)}\) is not unitary when \(f\) is constant.

topic-6-2-1.application: For each of the four functions, write \(U_f\bigl(\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\otimes\ket0\bigr)\), and say which results are entangled.
topic-6-2-1.challenge: With \(n\) input qubits in the uniform superposition and a clean target, \(U_f\) produces \(2^{-n/2}\sum_x\ket x\ket{f(x)}\). Measuring both registers gives a uniformly random \(x\) with \(f(x)\). About how many runs are needed, on average, before every value \(f(x)\) has been seen?

topic-6-2-2.foundation: Measure both registers of \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). What are the possible results and their probabilities? How many function values does one run reveal?
topic-6-2-2.application: To decide constant or balanced, we repeatedly prepare \((\ket{0,f(0)}+\ket{1,f(1)})/\sqrt2\) and measure both registers until both inputs have been seen. How many runs does this take on average?
topic-6-2-2.challenge: Show that measuring only the input register of \((\ket{0,f(0)}+\ket{1,f(1)})/\sqrt2\) gives \(0\) and \(1\) with probability \(1/2\) each for all four functions.

topic-6-2-3.foundation: For \(f=(0,1)\), apply \(H\) to the input of \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), and find the probability of each input outcome.
topic-6-2-3.application: For the constant function \(f=(0,0)\), repeat the calculation: start from \(\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\otimes\ket0\), apply \(U_f\), then \(H\) to the input.
topic-6-2-3.challenge: Combining the two previous problems, design a one-query procedure with a clean target that never wrongly answers “balanced.” With what probability does it detect a balanced function?

topic-6-3-1.application: Find every state that \(X\) leaves unchanged apart from a factor, by solving \(X(a,b)^T=\lambda(a,b)^T\).
topic-6-3-1.challenge: The target is prepared in \(\cos\theta\ket0+\sin\theta\ket1\), with real \(\theta\), and the oracle flips it. Show that its overlap with the original target is \(\sin2\theta\), and that the target keeps no record of the flip only when it is \(\ket+\) or \(\ket-\).

topic-6-3-2.application: Prepare the input in \(\ket+\), but mistakenly prepare the target in \(\ket+\) too. Find the output of \(U_f\) for each of the four functions. Does leaving the target unentangled suffice to obtain useful phase kickback?
topic-6-3-2.challenge: With \(n\) input qubits and the target in \(\ket-\), show that \(U_f\bigl(2^{-n/2}\sum_x\ket x\bigr)\ket-=\bigl(2^{-n/2}\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\bigr)\ket-\), and that the target ends in \(\ket-\) for every \(f\).

topic-6-3-3.foundation: For \(f(x)=x\), computed into a clean answer bit by CNOT, compute \(\mathrm{CNOT}\,(I\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\) on \(\ket{0,0}\) and \(\ket{1,0}\).
topic-6-3-3.application: Compute \(\mathrm{CNOT}\,(I\otimes Z)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\) on all four basis states, and identify the operation. Why does compute, phase, uncompute need the workspace to start at \(0\)?
topic-6-3-3.challenge: Omit the uncomputation: compute \(f(x)=x\) into the answer bit with CNOT and apply \(Z\) to the answer bit, but do not run CNOT again. Starting from \(\ket+\ket0\), apply \(H\) to the input at the end. Show that the outcome is random, whereas with uncomputation it is certain.

topic-6-4-1.application: For each of the four functions, compute the final input amplitudes \((s_0+s_1)/2\) and \((s_0-s_1)/2\).
topic-6-4-1.challenge: Show that if the final \(H\) is omitted, or replaced by \(X\), the measurement gives \(0\) and \(1\) with probability \(1/2\) each, for every function.

topic-6-4-2.foundation: Count the queries and the other operations in Deutsch’s algorithm, starting from \(\ket{00}\).
topic-6-4-2.application: Run Deutsch’s algorithm for \(f=(1,0)\), giving the state after each step.
topic-6-4-2.challenge: With \(n\) input qubits, after the query and \(H\) applied to each input qubit, show that the amplitude of the input configuration \(0^n\) is \(2^{-n}\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\). Deduce that one query distinguishes constant from balanced functions with certainty.

topic-6-4-3.foundation: Name the four stages of Deutsch’s algorithm and the operations used in each.
topic-6-4-3.application: Replace the target \(\ket-\) by \(\ket+\), and run the algorithm for \(f=(0,1)\). What does the measurement give?
topic-6-4-3.challenge: Leave out the first \(H\) on the input, so that the input stays \(\ket0\). Show that the algorithm then gives each outcome with probability \(1/2\) for every function.

topic-7-1-1.foundation: A predicate on three-bit labels marks the labels whose bits add to \(2\). How many labels are marked, and what is the probability that a uniformly random label is marked?
topic-7-1-1.application: One label among \(N=8\) is marked. A classical search queries labels in a uniformly random order, without repetition, until it finds the marked one. What is the expected number of queries?
topic-7-1-1.challenge: One label among \(N\) is marked, in a uniformly random position. Show that any classical algorithm making \(k\) queries finds it with probability at most \(k/N\).

topic-7-1-2.foundation: For \(N=4\) with the label \(01\) marked, write the amplitudes after preparing the uniform superposition and applying the phase oracle.
topic-7-1-2.application: For \(N=8\) with one marked label, what are the amplitudes after preparation and marking, and what is the probability of measuring the marked label?
topic-7-1-2.challenge: Show that applying the phase oracle any number of times, with nothing in between, never changes any measurement probability.

topic-7-1-3.foundation: Reflect the amplitudes \(\tfrac12(1,-1,1,1)\) about their mean.
topic-7-1-3.application: For \(N=8\) with one marked label, compute the amplitudes after one marking and one reflection about the mean, and the success probability.
topic-7-1-3.challenge: Show directly from \(a_x\mapsto2\mu-a_x\) that reflection about the mean preserves the sum of squared amplitudes, for real amplitudes.

topic-7-2-1.foundation: For \(N=8\) with the marked labels \(011\) and \(101\), write \(\ket G\) and \(\ket B\).
topic-7-2-1.application: For \(N=8\) and \(M=2\), write \(\ket s\) as a combination of \(\ket G\) and \(\ket B\).
topic-7-2-1.challenge: Show that the oracle \(O_f\) and the reflection \(D=2\ket s\bra s-I\) both map the plane of \(\ket G\) and \(\ket B\) into itself, by computing their action on \(\ket G\) and \(\ket B\).

topic-7-2-2.foundation: Find the angle \(\theta\) for \(N=16\) with \(M=1\), and for \(N=8\) with \(M=2\).
topic-7-2-2.application: For \(N=8\) and \(M=2\), how many iterations give success with certainty?
topic-7-2-2.challenge: Show that, for \(0\lt M\lt N\), exactly one Grover iteration gives certain success precisely when \(M/N=1/4\).

topic-7-2-3.foundation: For \(N=16\) and \(M=1\), by how many degrees does each Grover iteration rotate the state?
topic-7-2-3.application: For \(N=16\) and \(M=1\), give the angle of the state and the success probability after \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), and \(4\) iterations.
topic-7-2-3.challenge: In the plane with the bad direction as the first axis and the good direction as the second, reflection across the line at angle \(\alpha\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\alpha&\sin2\alpha\\\sin2\alpha&-\cos2\alpha\end{pmatrix}\). Verify that reflecting across the bad axis and then across \(\ket s\) is a rotation by \(2\theta\).

topic-7-3-1.application: For \(N=64\) and \(M=1\), which number of iterations maximizes the success probability, and what is that probability?
topic-7-3-1.challenge: Show that, given success, the measured label is uniformly distributed over the \(M\) marked labels, and that, given failure, it is uniform over the unmarked labels.

topic-7-3-2.foundation: For \(N=4\) and \(M=1\), compute the success probability after three iterations.
topic-7-3-2.application: A search has \(N=16\) items. You plan three Grover iterations assuming one marked item, but there are actually four. What success probability do three iterations give? How many iterations would work if you knew there were four?
topic-7-3-2.challenge: Show that the sequence of success probabilities \(p_0,p_1,p_2,\dots\) is periodic when \(\theta\) is a rational multiple of \(\pi\), and find the period for \(N=4\), \(M=1\).

topic-7-3-3.foundation: An algorithm succeeds with probability \(p\) per attempt and checks its candidate with one query. How many attempts does it need on average to find a marked label?
topic-7-3-3.application: For \(N=1024\), the iteration count tuned for \(M=1\) is \(k=25\). What is the success probability if in fact \(M=4\)?
topic-7-3-3.challenge: Each verified attempt succeeds with probability at least \(1/4\), independently. Show that \(t\) attempts all fail with probability at most \((3/4)^t\), and find the smallest \(t\) for which this is below \(10^{-6}\).

topic-7-4-1.foundation: A preparation succeeds with probability \(p=1/9\). Find \(\theta\) and the amplitudes of \(\ket G\) and \(\ket B\).
topic-7-4-1.application: For \(p=1/9\), how many amplification iterations maximize success, and what is the success probability?
topic-7-4-1.challenge: A one-qubit preparation \(A\) gives \(A\ket0=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\ket0+\tfrac12\ket1\), and success means outcome \(1\). Show that one amplification iteration succeeds with certainty, even though this preparation is not uniform.

topic-7-4-2.foundation: For \(A=H\) on one qubit, write \(R_\psi=A(2\ket0\bra0-I)A^\dagger\) as a matrix.
topic-7-4-2.application: Show that \(A(2\ket0\bra0-I)A^\dagger=2\ket\psi\bra\psi-I\) when \(A\ket0=\ket\psi\), and that it is unitary.
topic-7-4-2.challenge: Why can the reflection \(R_\psi\) not be replaced by measuring whether the prepared state succeeded? Show that measuring after each oracle step makes the success probability stay at \(p\).

topic-7-4-3.foundation: For \(p=0.01\), compare the number of independent trials needed for a reasonable chance of success with the number of amplification iterations.
topic-7-4-3.application: Preparing \(A\) costs \(100\) gates and the success test \(20\) gates. For \(p=10^{-4}\), compare the total cost of about \(1/p\) independent trials, each a preparation and a test, with about \(\tfrac\pi4/\sqrt p\) amplification iterations, each using \(A\), \(A^\dagger\), and the test.
topic-7-4-3.challenge: Preparing an arbitrary list of \(N\) amplitudes costs about \(N\) gates. For a search among \(N\) items with one marked item, so that \(p=1/N\), compare the cost of amplitude amplification with a classical scan of the list.

topic-8-1-1.foundation: A circuit applies \(H\) to qubit 1, then \(X\) to qubit 2, then CNOT with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target, starting from \(\ket{00}\). Write the state after each step.
topic-8-1-1.application: Apply, to \(\ket{00}\), first \(H\) on qubit 1 and then CNOT, and in the other order. Do the two operations commute?
topic-8-1-1.challenge: Prove that \((U\otimes I)(I\otimes V)=(I\otimes V)(U\otimes I)=U\otimes V\): gates on different wires commute.

topic-8-1-2.foundation: In the four-item search circuit, how many oracle uses and how many Hadamard gates does one Grover iteration contain, and how many Hadamard gates prepare the start?
topic-8-1-2.application: List the gates of Deutsch’s algorithm in time order, starting from \(\ket{00}\), with the qubits each acts on.
topic-8-1-2.challenge: An oracle box \(O_f\) on \(n\) qubits marks one fixed string. It is built from \(X\) gates and a phase flip controlled on all \(n\) qubits, which in turn uses Toffoli gates and \(n-2\) workspace qubits. Count the gates in such a construction.

topic-8-1-3.foundation: Bob receives a bit \(b\) and applies \(X\) only if \(b=1\). Write his operation for each value of \(b\).
topic-8-1-3.application: For the input \((\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1)\ket0\), compare (a) CNOT followed by measuring the control with (b) measuring the control first and then applying \(X\) to the target if the result is \(1\). Show that the outcomes and final states agree.
topic-8-1-3.challenge: Now the control is not measured at the end. Compare CNOT with “measure the control, then apply \(X\) if \(1\)” on the input \(\ket+\ket-\), by applying \(H\) to the control afterward and measuring it.

topic-8-2-1.foundation: Compute \(R_X(\pi)\) and \(R_Z(\pi)\), and compare them with \(X\) and \(Z\).
topic-8-2-1.application: Verify by multiplying matrices that \(HZH=X\), \(HXH=Z\), \(S^2=Z\), and \(T^2=S\).
topic-8-2-1.challenge: Show that \(R_Z(\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\theta/2},e^{i\theta/2})\), and that up to a global phase it is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})\). Which values of \(\theta\) give \(S\) and \(T\)?

topic-8-2-2.foundation: Apply controlled-\(Z\) to the four basis states. Show that exchanging the roles of control and target gives the same operation.
topic-8-2-2.application: Verify that \((I\otimes H)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\,(I\otimes H)\) acts as controlled-\(Z\) on \(\ket{10}\) and \(\ket{11}\).
topic-8-2-2.challenge: Let \(\ket v\) be an eigenvector of \(U\) with \(U\ket v=e^{i\phi}\ket v\). Show that controlled-\(U\) sends \(\ket+\ket v\) to \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+e^{i\phi}\ket1)\otimes\ket v\). Is the result entangled?

topic-8-2-3.foundation: Which gates mark the string \(01\) on two qubits, that is, multiply \(\ket{01}\) by \(-1\) and leave the other basis states alone?
topic-8-2-3.application: For two qubits, verify that \((H\otimes H)(2\ket{00}\bra{00}-I)(H\otimes H)\) and \(2\ket s\bra s-I\) agree on \(\ket{00}\).
topic-8-2-3.challenge: Show that \((X\otimes X)\,CZ\,(X\otimes X)=-(2\ket{00}\bra{00}-I)\). Why does this sign not matter in an ordinary Grover iteration, and when would it matter?

topic-8-3-1.foundation: Apply \(H\otimes H\) to \(\ket{00}\), and check that the result is a product state.
topic-8-3-1.application: A circuit applies \(H\) to qubit 1, then \(X\) to qubit 2, then \(H\) to qubit 1 again. Find the result on \(\ket{00}\), and explain why it had to be a product state.
topic-8-3-1.challenge: Show that one-qubit operations cannot turn an entangled two-qubit state into a product state.

topic-8-3-2.foundation: Which of these gate sets can prepare a Bell state from \(\ket{00}\): \(\{H,X,Z\}\); \(\{H,\text{CNOT}\}\); \(\{\text{CNOT},X\}\)?
topic-8-3-2.application: Show that circuits of CNOT and \(X\) gates only permute computational basis states.
topic-8-3-2.challenge: A reversible circuit on \(m\) wires uses \(g\) gates, each an \(X\), CNOT, or Toffoli on chosen wires. Show that there are at most \((3m^3)^g\) such circuits, and deduce that most Boolean functions of \(n\) bits need at least about \(2^n/\log_2(3m^3)\) gates.

topic-8-3-3.foundation: Each of \(1000\) gates is approximated within \(10^{-6}\). What error bound holds for the whole circuit?
topic-8-3-3.application: A circuit has \(10^6\) gates and its total error must be at most \(10^{-2}\). What accuracy must each gate have if the error is split equally?

topic-8-4-1.foundation: A circuit on three qubits applies \(H\) to each qubit, then CNOT from qubit 1 to qubit 2, then CNOT from qubit 2 to qubit 3. Give its gate count, depth, and width.
topic-8-4-1.application: Compute the AND of \(n=8\) bits with a chain of Toffoli gates: \(w_1=x_1x_2\), \(w_2=w_1x_3\), and so on, then the output, then uncompute the workspace. Give the gate count, depth, and width.
topic-8-4-1.challenge: Compute the AND of the same \(8\) bits with a balanced tree instead: combine bits in pairs, then pairs of results, and so on. Compare gate count, depth, and workspace with the chain.

topic-8-4-2.foundation: Three qubits sit on a line, \(1\)–\(2\)–\(3\), and only neighbours can interact. How many SWAP gates are needed to apply a CNOT between qubits 1 and 3 and restore the original placement?
topic-8-4-2.application: A SWAP gate costs three CNOT gates. Count the CNOT gates in the construction above, and for a CNOT between the two ends of a line of \(n\) qubits.
topic-8-4-2.challenge: A data set of \(N=2^n\) numbers is loaded into amplitudes using one gate per number, and then searched with about \(\sqrt N\) queries. When does the quadratic query speedup survive in the total cost?

topic-8-4-3.foundation: Each gate fails independently with probability \(10^{-3}\). What is the probability that a circuit of \(1000\) gates runs without any failure?
topic-8-4-3.application: How small must the failure probability per gate be for a circuit of \(10^9\) gates to run without failure with probability at least \(0.9\)?
topic-8-4-3.challenge: A repetition code stores a classical bit as three identical bits and decodes by majority. With independent flip probability \(0<q<1\), derive the failure probability and find when encoding helps. Now consider \(\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\): what does a phase flip \(Z\) on its first qubit do, and why does majority voting miss it?

topic-9-1-1.foundation: How many bits does \(N=10^9\) have in binary? A procedure takes about \(\sqrt N\) steps. Is that polynomial in the input length?
topic-9-1-1.application: An algorithm takes \(5\) steps on half of the \(n\)-bit inputs and \(2^n\) steps on the other half. Give its worst-case cost and its average cost over uniformly random inputs.
topic-9-1-1.challenge: Trial division finds a factor of \(N\) by testing the divisors \(2,3,\dots,\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\). Express its worst-case number of divisions in terms of the input length \(n=\log_2N\). Is it polynomial-time?

topic-9-1-2.foundation: Is \(100n=O(n^2)\)? Is \(n^2=O(100n)\)? Give constants, or explain why none exist.
topic-9-1-2.application: Two algorithms take exactly \(1000n\) and \(n^2\) steps. Which is faster at \(n=100\), \(n=1000\), and \(n=10{,}000\)? Which scales better? Explain why these are different questions.
topic-9-1-2.challenge: For which input lengths \(n\geq2\) is an algorithm costing \(n^{10}\) steps faster than one costing \(2^n\) steps? What does this show about asymptotic comparisons?

topic-9-1-3.foundation: A Grover search over \(N=10^6\) items uses about \((\pi/4)\sqrt N\) queries. If each query costs \(1000\) gates and each reflection \(50\) gates, estimate the total gate count.
topic-9-1-3.application: A classical scan costs one operation per item. For \(N=10^6\), below which cost \(c\) per query does a Grover search, costing about \((\pi/4)\sqrt N\cdot c\) gates, beat the scan?
topic-9-1-3.challenge: Algorithm A uses \(n^2\) queries and \(n^3\) other gates; algorithm B uses \(n\) queries and \(n^4\) other gates. If each query costs \(n^k\) gates, which algorithm has the smaller total gate count, depending on \(k\)?

topic-9-2-1.foundation: Which of these are decision problems: (a) is \(N\) prime? (b) find a factor of \(N\); (c) does a graph \(G\) contain a path from \(u\) to \(v\)?
topic-9-2-1.application: For the problem “does \(N\) have a factor \(d\) with \(1\lt d\lt k\)?”, give a witness for \(N=91\) and \(k=10\), and explain how a witness is checked in polynomial time.
topic-9-2-1.challenge: Prove that if \(A\) reduces to \(B\) in polynomial time and \(B\) is in P, then \(A\) is in P. Why must the reduction itself run in polynomial time?

topic-9-2-2.foundation: An algorithm errs with probability at most \(1/3\). Run it three times independently and take the majority answer. What is the error probability?
topic-9-2-2.application: How many independent runs, with a majority vote, bring the error below \(0.01\) when each run errs with probability \(1/3\)?
topic-9-2-2.challenge: Show that an algorithm that ignores its input and answers by flipping a fair coin has error \(1/2\) on every input, and that majority voting over repeated runs never improves it. Why is the condition “error at most \(1/3\)” essential?

topic-9-2-3.foundation: Trial division of a \(2048\)-bit number may test up to \(\sqrt N\approx2^{1024}\) divisors. Write this roughly as a power of ten.
topic-9-2-3.application: A rough estimate for Shor’s factoring algorithm is \(n^3\) operations for an \(n\)-bit number. Compare \(n^3\) with \(2^{n/2}\) for \(n=2048\).
topic-9-2-3.challenge: The best known classical factoring method, the number field sieve, takes time roughly \(\exp\bigl(1.92(\ln N)^{1/3}(\ln\ln N)^{2/3}\bigr)\). Evaluate it for a \(2048\)-bit \(N\), and explain why this comparison does not prove that quantum computers are exponentially more powerful.

topic-9-3-1.foundation: Which of these establishes a lower bound on query complexity: (a) an algorithm using \(\sqrt N\) queries; (b) a proof that every algorithm needs at least \(\sqrt N\) queries; (c) many failed attempts to find an algorithm with fewer queries?
topic-9-3-1.application: Using the fact that \(k\) classical queries find a single marked item among \(N\) with probability at most \(k/N\), show that success probability \(1/2\) needs at least \(N/2\) queries.
topic-9-3-1.challenge: In the query model, an algorithm may compute without limit between queries. Explain why a query lower bound still applies to algorithms with limited computation, but a query upper bound need not give a fast algorithm.

topic-9-3-2.foundation: For \(N=10^6\), compare Grover’s query count, about \((\pi/4)\sqrt N\), with the classical average \(N/2\).
topic-9-3-2.application: If some quantum algorithm searched with only \(N^{1/3}\) queries, how many would it use for \(N=10^6\)? Which result rules this out?
topic-9-3-2.challenge: Use the lower bound to show that no quantum algorithm finds a marked item among \(N=2^n\) with a number of queries polynomial in \(n\). What does this imply for solving NP problems by unstructured search?

topic-9-3-3.foundation: After \(T=3\) queries, what is the largest possible degree of an amplitude, and of an acceptance probability?
topic-9-3-3.application: The approximate degree of OR on \(N\) bits grows like \(\sqrt N\). For \(N=10^4\), what lower bound on queries does \(T\geq d/2\) give, up to a constant factor?
topic-9-3-3.challenge: Show that the exact degree of OR on \(N\) bits is \(N\), by writing \(\mathrm{OR}(z)=1-\prod_i(1-z_i)\). What does this imply for algorithms that must be correct with certainty?

topic-9-4-1.foundation: For Deutsch’s algorithm and for Grover search, name the property that is encoded in phases, and the operation that turns it into probability.
topic-9-4-1.application: For each of the two algorithms, list costs that its query count does not include.
topic-9-4-1.challenge: An algorithm prepares the uniform superposition of \(n\) qubits, applies an oracle once, and measures immediately. Show that it does no better than one classical query, whether the oracle is a phase oracle or the reversible \(U_f\).

topic-9-4-2.foundation: Can a quantum computer decide the halting problem? Why not?
topic-9-4-2.application: A classical simulation of an \(n\)-qubit circuit stores all \(2^n\) amplitudes. How does its memory grow, and why does the simulation nevertheless show that quantum computers compute nothing beyond Turing machines?
topic-9-4-2.challenge: A source promises to prepare either \(\ket0\) on every run or \(\ket+\) on every run. After obtaining \(k\) copies, the alternatives are \(\ket0^{\otimes k}\) and \(\ket+^{\otimes k}\). Compute their overlap. Can any finite number of copies guarantee perfect discrimination? How does that differ from making the error very small?

topic-9-4-3.application: Use the period \(r=4\) of \(2^x\bmod15\) to factor \(15\), by computing \(\gcd(2^{r/2}-1,15)\) and \(\gcd(2^{r/2}+1,15)\).
topic-9-4-3.challenge: Let \(a^x\bmod N\) have even period \(r\), with \(a^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\pmod N\). Show that \(\gcd(a^{r/2}-1,N)\) is a factor of \(N\) other than \(1\) and \(N\).

appendix-a.foundation: Design a two-state finite automaton that accepts the binary strings with an even number of \(1\)s, and trace it on \(1011\).
appendix-a.application: Run the stack procedure on \(aaabbb\) and on \(aabbb\), giving the stack height after each symbol.
appendix-a.challenge: Show that no finite automaton recognizes the strings over \(\{a,b\}\) with equal numbers of \(a\)’s and \(b\)’s, in any order.

appendix-b.foundation: Derive \(aaabbb\) from \(S\) with the rules \(S\to aSb\) and \(S\to\epsilon\), writing each step.
appendix-b.application: Reduce \((\lambda x.\lambda y.x)\,a\,b\) step by step.
appendix-b.challenge: With Church numerals, show that \(\mathrm{SUCC}=\lambda n.\lambda f.\lambda x.f(n\,f\,x)\) applied to \(2=\lambda f.\lambda x.f(f\,x)\) gives \(3\).

appendix-c.foundation: What is the operator norm of \(\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\), and of a unitary \(U\)?
appendix-c.challenge: Show that a projector \(P\), with \(P^2=P=P^\dagger\), has only the eigenvalues \(0\) and \(1\), and that \(I-P\) is also a projector.

appendix-d.foundation: Write the density matrix of the ensemble that prepares \(\ket0\) with probability \(3/4\) and \(\ket1\) with probability \(1/4\). What is the probability of outcome \(0\)?
appendix-d.application: Show that the ensembles \(\{\ket0,\ket1\}\) and \(\{\ket+,\ket-\}\), each with equal probabilities, have the same density matrix.
appendix-d.challenge: For the measurement with effects \(E_0=c\ket-\bra-\), \(E_+=c\ket1\bra1\), and \(E_?=I-E_0-E_+\), where \(c=1/(1+1/\sqrt2)\), compute the probability of the inconclusive outcome for \(\ket0\) and for \(\ket+\).

appendix-e.foundation: With two hidden bits and the query \(\ket{i,b}\mapsto\ket{i,b\oplus z_i}\), start from \(\ket{1,0}\). Write the amplitudes after one query as polynomials in \(z_1,z_2\).
appendix-e.application: Use \(z_i^2=z_i\) on Boolean inputs to reduce \(z_1^2z_2+z_1z_2^2\) to a multilinear polynomial.
appendix-e.challenge: Write the parity of two bits, \(z_1\oplus z_2\), as a real polynomial, and show that its degree is \(2\). What lower bound on queries does this give for an exact algorithm, and is it achieved?
